# Organic Chemistry I

## Core ideas and reasoning

Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds. Carbon forms four bonds and can build chains, branches and rings. A homologous series has the same functional group and general formula with successive members differing by CH₂; chemical behaviour is similar while physical properties change gradually. Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with only carbon-carbon single bonds and formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ for open chains. Alkenes contain a carbon-carbon double bond and open-chain monoalkenes have formula CₙH₂ₙ. Name a chain by its carbon count and the functional group, locating multiple bonds when needed. Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different connectivity. Alkenes decolourise bromine water by addition, while alkanes do not under ordinary test conditions without ultraviolet light. Alkanes can undergo substitution with halogens under ultraviolet light. Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water; insufficient oxygen may produce carbon monoxide and soot. Draw structures with every carbon having four bonds, and balance equations using atom counts.

## Worked practice

### Example 1

State the general formulas for open-chain alkanes and monoalkenes.

Alkanes: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Monoalkenes: CₙH₂ₙ, with one C=C double bond and no rings.

### Example 2

Describe how bromine water distinguishes ethene from ethane under ordinary conditions without ultraviolet light.

Ethene rapidly decolourises bromine water through addition at the double bond. Ethane does not under these test conditions.

### Example 3

Write the complete combustion equation for ethane.

2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen counts balance.

## Check your reasoning

Explain why the method applies before calculating or naming a result. Compare with a contrasting case. For calculations carry units, keep intermediate precision, then check by substitution, conservation or a second route. Describe observations separately from their explanation.
